questions.explanation: A unit is a label attached to a number to say what has been measured, and the label carries as much information as the digits do. The metre, the second, and the kilogram measure different things, so two numbers carrying different units cannot be added or compared at all. This is why a result without a unit is incomplete: the number 9 might be nine metres of length or nine seconds of duration, and nothing in the digits distinguishes them. The common failure is to treat a bare number as if the unit were decoration, which is how answers go wrong when a question switches units halfway through.

questions.explanation: A prefix is a fixed power of ten attached to a unit, and it multiplies the unit by that power without changing what is being measured. questions.explanation: The empirical rule is a description of a normal distribution, and it is built around the mean and the standard deviation, which for such a distribution fix the whole shape. Roughly two thirds of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent within two, and about 99.7 percent within three, with the counts growing the further from the centre one goes. The interval is found by adding and subtracting that many standard deviations from the mean, so a mean of 70 and a spread of 8 put the two-standard-deviation band from 54 to 86. The rule is not a law about data in general: for a skewed or flat set the proportions do not hold at all, which is the limitation worth stating whenever it is used.

answer.exemplar: An index number on its own is a ratio, and a ratio has no absolute meaning, because it says only that one figure is larger or smaller than another by a stated factor. A reading of 120 tells the reader that the quantity now stands at 1.2 times whatever it stood at in the period assigned the value 100, and it says nothing at all about the size of either. That is why the base period must always travel with the series: the same quantity could be given an index of 120 against one base and 240 against another, simply by halving the second base figure, and both would be arithmetically correct. The conventional choice of 100 for the base is what makes the reading directly readable as a percentage change, so a base of 1 would convey exactly the same information while being far less convenient. The choice of base also determines how the series reads across time, since a base year with an unusually large value makes every later year look like a decline, so publishers fix the base and hold it for the life of the series. Anyone reading an index number without its base is therefore reading a number whose meaning has been left out.

questions.explanation: A strong answer grounds the point in the arbitrariness of the base, for instance by noting that halving the base figure doubles every later reading, and that the convention of 100 exists so readings read as percentages. It should also observe that the choice of base year affects how the whole series reads, since an extreme base year flatters or depresses everything after it. An answer that only says the base must be stated is right but leaves the reader unable to see why, which is the part the question is really asking for.
questions.hint: Ask what a reading of 120 would become if the base figure were changed to 50.

answer.exemplar: The empirical rule is a description of one particular shape of distribution, and it holds only for the normal one, so the shape of the data has to be established before the rule may be used. For a normal distribution the rule says that roughly 68 percent of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent within two, and about 99.7 percent within three, and the reason is that the mean and the standard deviation then determine the whole shape, so the two facts fix the curve. With a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 8, the one-spread band runs from 62 to 78, the two-spread band from 54 to 86, and the three-spread band from 46 to 94. The failure mode is a data set that is skewed or flat, where a mean and a spread still exist but do not determine the distribution, and there the true coverage can be far from the advertised figure, sometimes much lower in the tails than the rule promises. A second limitation is that the rule says nothing about the shape between those marks, so it cannot be used to place a single value precisely, only to bound a share of the data.

questions.explanation: The answer has to state the distributional assumption, since that is the whole reason the rule can fail, and ideally say what kinds of data break it. Listing the three bands with a worked mean and spread shows the rule actually applied rather than recited. It should also make clear the rule concerns shares of data and not the position of any single value, since the frequent misuse is to place one measurement at 1.96 spreads and call it almost certain, which the rule does not license. An answer that gives the bands without naming the assumption leaves the main limitation unstated.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true of the shape of the data before the bands mean anything.
questions.learningObjective: explain what the empirical rule assumes about the shape of data

answer.exemplar: A bar chart draws each bar as a length measured from the value at the bottom of the axis, and when that value is zero the length is proportional to the value it represents. The proportionality is the whole point, since it is what lets a reader compare bars by eye. If the axis instead begins at 90, every bar is 90 units longer than it would otherwise be, and that common 90 is added to each bar rather than scaled with it, so the ratio between two bar lengths is no longer the ratio between the two values. Two values of 95 and 105, differing by about 11 percent, are drawn as bars of 5 units and 15 units, which differ by a factor of three. The exaggeration grows as the axis minimum rises: a chart beginning at 99 would make a change from 99 to 100 look enormous. A truncated axis is not dishonest in itself, and it is often the only way to show small differences at all, but the reader has to be told, because a claim that one bar is several times another is a claim about values and not about the picture. Reading the axis before reading the bars is the habit that prevents the error.

questions.explanation: A good answer locates the mechanism in the common offset added to every bar, and works the numbers so the exaggeration is visible rather than asserted. It should also say when a truncated axis is acceptable, since the useful conclusion is about labelling and reading habits rather than a blanket ban, and an answer that only condemns truncated axes is not right, since small differences cannot be shown otherwise. The closing point about reading the axis before the bars is what makes the explanation usable.
questions.hint: Ask what every bar gains when the axis stops short of zero.
questions.learningObjective: explain how a truncated axis distorts a comparison of bar lengths

answer.exemplar: Units fix what kind of quantity a number describes, and every valid operation on measured quantities is one that respects those kinds. A flow rate is one quantity per unit of another, so dividing a volume by a time gives litres per second, and 300 litres in 20 seconds is 15 litres per second. Multiplying instead of dividing leaves a product of units rather than a rate, so 300 times 20 is 6000 litre-seconds, and a litre-second is not a rate at all: it says how much volume and how much time were involved without saying how one related to the other. The claim that the pump delivers 6000 litres per second therefore fails on units before any question of arithmetic arises, and no choice of numbers can rescue it, because the error is in the kind of quantity asserted. This is the strength of the dimensional check. It catches whole families of mistakes at once, a lost factor of a thousand among them, since an equation can be numerically wrong and dimensionally right, but an equation that is dimensionally wrong cannot be right at any value of the numbers. It is worth noting its limit as well: units alone will not catch a genuine mistake that happens to preserve the kinds, such as substituting the radius for the diameter in a circumference formula, where both sides remain lengths.

questions.explanation: The answer must do the division to get the real rate, show what the multiplication produces instead, and name that result as a product of units rather than a rate, since that contrast is the argument. Stating the limit of the check, that it cannot catch an error which happens to preserve the units, distinguishes a considered answer from an enthusiastic one. Without the worked numbers the explanation asserts rather than demonstrates, and without the limitation it overclaims a method that is powerful but not infallible.
questions.hint: Compute the rate the correct way, then see what kind of quantity the claimed one actually is.
questions.learningObjective: explain how units can show that a claimed quantity is impossible
